discovery: Quantum cryptography: the invention of quantum key distribution and entanglement-based secure communication

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the quantum no-cloning principle and the disturbance caused by measurement make provably secure key distribution possible. That turned a foundational feature of quantum mechanics into a physical resource. Ekert (E91) then linked the security of a key directly to the violation of Bell's inequality, so that entanglement and nonlocality became the basis of cryptography. This idea led on to device-independent security. These insights started the field of quantum information. They prompted a generation of experiments: fibre and free-space links, entanglement distribution, and intercontinental satellite QKD. Bennett and Brassard also co-invented quantum teleportation, which many laboratories have since realised. Their work showed that quantum physics is not only something to be tested but a new way of handling information. It changed physics laboratories around the world and gave rise to a global quantum communication technology.
